claims.text: The feedstock is fine FeCoNiCrAl HEA powder with a particle size of 5–30 μm.
The FeCoNiCrAl powder contains Al-rich and Cr-rich microsegregated regions.
The initial FeCoNiCrAl material has a BCC random-solid-solution structure.
The substrate is grit-blasted Inconel 718 with a surface roughness of approximately Ra = 3.9 μm.
A roughly 150 μm FeCoNiCrAl bond coat will be deposited using a low-temperature ID-HVAF i7 torch at a medium air/fuel-pressure setting.
The deposition uses propylene fuel, a 63 mm 3L4 nozzle, a 2.75 mm powder injector, and substrate preheating to 155 °C.
The medium-pressure process will produce a coating with approximately 0.2% porosity.
The medium-pressure process will produce uniform elemental distribution while retaining the BCC structure.
The resulting coating will have a minimal interdiffusion zone of approximately 3 μm.
High-temperature exposure will form a thin, dense, continuous Al2O3 thermally grown oxide with limited mixed-oxide formation.
Low-temperature deposition minimizes in-flight and deposition-stage oxidation.
Low porosity and high coating density restrict oxygen ingress.
Limited porosity and sluggish elemental diffusion in the HEA favor protective alumina formation and inhibit internal oxidation and uncontrolled TGO growth.
The absence of reactive elements such as Y or Hf may increase scale-spallation risk under severe exposure conditions.

Relative to more porous or more deposition-oxidized coatings, the medium-pressure HVAF-i7 coating will exhibit slower TGO growth, reduced internal oxidation, and improved oxidation resistance during 50-hour isothermal exposure at 1000–1150 °C.
Coatings produced at low and high air/fuel-pressure settings have porosities of 0.8% and 1.8%, respectively.
The medium-pressure coating will have superior microstructure and oxidation behavior relative to low- or high-pressure coatings and literature HVAF-M3/MCrAlY systems.
The proposed benefit should remain effective under isothermal exposure for up to 50 hours between 1000 and 1150 °C.
Performance beyond 50 hours or under more severe thermal cycling may be limited by substrate melting or oxide-scale spallation.

Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in TGO thickness and internal oxidation, improved oxidation kinetics, or avoidance of significant spallation relative to baseline coatings would reject the hypothesis.
